title: Moving bees for orchard pollination
subtitle: Timing hive placement to maximise fruit set in apple and pear orchards.
excerpt: A hive placed in or beside an orchard at full bloom can dramatically increase fruit set. The colony needs to arrive when around twenty percent of the blossom is open, orientate over two days, and work the flower for the whole bloom period. Getting the placement and timing right matters more than the number of hives.
sourceNotes: NBU Beekeeper's Toolkit (2024), section on moving hives. BBKA advisory leaflet on orchard pollination. Cornell Cooperative Extension, Honey Bees and Fruit Tree Pollination (2019). AHDB Horticulture, Pollination of top fruit (2020).

glossaryTerms.definition: A formal or informal arrangement between a beekeeper and a grower, setting out the number of hives, placement dates, payment, and responsibilities during the pollination period.
The proportion of blossoms on a tree that develop into fruit after successful pollination. Poor fruit set means fewer apples or pears despite good flowering.

content.text: Moving bees into an orchard at blossom time is one of the most reliable ways to improve
fruit set

in apples, pears, and other tree fruit. A strong colony placed correctly at the right point in the bloom cycle can visit several million flowers in a fortnight. The practical decisions are when to move, where to site the hive, and how to agree a
pollination contract
with the grower if the arrangement is formal.
When to move

Place hives when around fifteen to twenty percent of the blossom on the target trees is open. This gives the colony two or three days to orientate to the new site while there is still a full bloom ahead of them. Move too early and bees orientate to pre-bloom scent and may shift their foraging elsewhere when the flowers open. Move at peak bloom and the colony misses the first and most important pollination window.

UK apple blossom typically runs from mid-April in Kent to mid-May in the north of England, depending on variety. Pears flower a week to ten days earlier than apples. Check with the grower which varieties are in the block and what their usual blossom window is.
How many hives

The standard recommendation for commercial top-fruit growing is one strong colony per hectare of orchard. For a home orchard of a dozen trees, a single well-populated colony is ample. Colony strength matters far more than the number of hives: a colony covering eight frames of brood is worth three weak five-frame colonies for pollination purposes.
Hive placement

Site hives at the edge of the orchard rather than inside it if the grower uses sprays. Spray applications during bloom are always a negotiation point: insecticides applied to open flowers kill pollinators.
Face the entrance toward the trees so foragers emerge directly into the orchard.
Site on level firm ground, away from livestock and machinery routes. Hives tipped or knocked mid-pollination are dangerous and the colony may abscond.
If moving more than one hive, space them at least 1.5 m apart. Drift between adjacent hives is significant when colonies are moved to a new site.
Moving the hives
Close the entrance after dark when all bees are in. Tape or staple a piece of foam across the opening: bees cannot chew through foam in transit and air still passes.
Strap the boxes together and to the transport vehicle. A hive that shifts in the van will arrive with the colony in shock.
Set the hive in position and open the entrance at the destination site immediately on arrival, even if it is still dark. Bees confined too long overheat.
Do not inspect the colony for two or three days after moving. Let bees orientate in peace before opening the hive.
The pollination contract
Even for an informal arrangement with a neighbouring grower, agree in writing:
Number of hives, minimum colony strength, and placement dates.
Any spraying that may happen during the pollination period and the expected notice. No spraying of open blossom with any pesticide should be allowed while bees are present.
Date when hives will be removed: typically when petal fall is complete.

attrs.cue: Bees are not foraging in the orchard despite warm weather
attrs.cause: Bees may still be orientating, or competing forage elsewhere is more attractive
attrs.fix: Wait three to four days after moving before judging activity. Watch the entrance at midday: returning foragers with pollen loads indicate they are working something, even if not the target crop.

attrs.cue: Mass bee mortality found near the hive during the pollination period
attrs.cause: Likely a spray event, even if not noticed
attrs.fix: Stop the arrangement, remove the hive, photograph the dead bees. Contact the grower immediately. A bee death sample can be sent to the National Bee Unit for pesticide analysis.
